summary: Presents an alternative way to do anti-replay checks and updates for IPsec AH and ESP. It avoids bit shifting and cuts the number of times the anti-replay window is adjusted. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A guard keeps a list of ticket numbers already used so nobody can reuse one. This shows a quicker way to keep that list without shuffling every entry each time.

questions: how to implement anti-replay without bit shifting
subtitle: An efficient IPsec anti-replay algorithm that avoids bit-shifting operations.

tldr.problem: IPsec's standard anti-replay algorithm uses bit-shifting to maintain a sliding window of accepted sequence numbers, which becomes very expensive on high-end multi-core processors that process thousands of packets in parallel with varying latencies.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6479 describes an alternative algorithm that organizes the window as a circular ring of blocks and only updates block indices instead of shifting bits, reducing the number of window adjustments by a factor of N (the block size).
tldr.outcome: High-performance network processors can now implement anti-replay more efficiently without interoperability impact, since the receiver can freely choose any compliant method and still accept packets from senders using the standard algorithm.

today: RFC 6479 remains an informational specification used by high-performance IPsec implementations to optimize anti-replay processing. It is not a mandatory standard—IPsec implementations are free to use either the standard algorithm or this alternative. The RFC has no newer versions and is not obsoleted.

sections.title: The Anti-Replay Problem
sections.content:
IPsec (IP Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload) defines an anti-replay service that protects against an attacker resending old packets. The receiver keeps a sliding window of accepted sequence numbers: packets whose sequence number is inside the window are checked against a bitmap to see if they have been seen before. Packets outside the window are rejected.

The sliding window is represented as a range [WB, WT] where WB is the low end and WT is the high end. When the receiver sees a packet with a sequence number S higher than WT, the window slides forward: WB and WT both increase by S-WT, so S becomes the new high end.

To make room for the new sequence numbers, the standard algorithm shifts the bits in the window by S-WT positions. For a window bigger than 64 bits (which modern processors often need due to parallel processing), this shifting becomes expensive. In normal operation, packets arrive mostly in order, so bit-shifting happens continuously with every incoming packet.

RFC 6479 provides an alternative that avoids this costly bit-shifting while maintaining the same security properties.
sections.eli5: IPsec watches for duplicate packets using a rolling list. Every time a new packet arrives beyond the end of the list, the list slides forward and new slots open up at the end. The old way shuffles every item. This shows how to do it faster.

sections.title: The Block-Based Algorithm
sections.content:
The new algorithm organizes the bitmap as a circular ring of blocks instead of a linear array. The window size W is split into M blocks (where M is a power of two), each containing N bits (also a power of two, such as 32 bits). The actual sliding window covers M-1 blocks, but the ring has M blocks total, so one block is always unused as a buffer.

When a packet with sequence number S arrives that is higher than WT, the algorithm:

  • Adds S-WT to both WT and WB (shifting the window logically, not the bits)
  • If S is in a different block than WT, initializes all the bits in the new block(s) to zero without any shifting

The bit location in the bitmap is calculated directly from the lowest N bits of the sequence number, and the block index comes from the next M bits. This means the check does not depend on WB; it only depends on S. The algorithm is faster because it does not shift bits—it only updates the block index and clears blocks as needed.

The cost is a small amount of extra memory for the redundant block, but this is minimal for large window sizes. For a window of 1024 bits using 32-bit blocks, one extra block uses only 4 bytes.
sections.eli5: Instead of shifting bits, the new way uses a circular list of blocks. When the window slides, it just clears the blocks that moved out and marks them ready for new numbers. Finding which block and bit to check is fast because the sequence number tells you directly.

sections.title: Implementation Example
sections.content:
RFC 6479 provides complete C code for checking and updating the anti-replay window. The code shows two functions: ipsec_check_replay_window() checks if an incoming packet is a duplicate, and ipsec_update_replay_window() updates the window after a packet is authenticated.

The implementation assumes a 1024-bit hidden window with 32 redundant bits, giving a supported window of 992 bits on a 32-bit microprocessor. The algorithm first checks if the sequence number is larger than the highest seen so far (always valid). Then it checks if the sequence number is too old (outside the window). Finally, if it is inside the window, it computes the bit location and block index directly from the sequence number and checks or sets the corresponding bit.

The code is straightforward and requires no external dependencies. Comments in the RFC explain the constraints and how the algorithm scales to different microprocessor architectures (32-bit, 64-bit, cache-line-aligned, etc.).
sections.eli5: The RFC includes working code that an engineer can copy into their IPsec software. It shows exactly how to check if a packet is old, how to check if it is a duplicate, and how to update the list after accepting a packet.

sections.title: Performance Gains
sections.content:
The primary benefit of this algorithm is a reduction in the number of window updates. With a block size of N bits, the number of block-clear operations drops to 1/N times that of the bit-shifting algorithm. For a 32-bit block on a 32-bit processor, this means 32 times fewer updates in normal in-order packet processing.

The bit-checking operation is actually faster because it does not depend on WB. Instead of computing location = S - WB, the code computes bit_location = S & BITMAP_LOC_MASK (a simple bitwise AND). This is a single CPU instruction instead of a subtraction and division.

The trade-off is memory: the circular buffer needs one extra block. For most window sizes, this is negligible (a few bytes to a few hundred bytes). The RFC notes that the unused bits in the buffer block can sometimes be repurposed, offsetting the cost further.

RFC 4302 and RFC 4303 allow window sizes of 32 or 64 bits, but high-end processors often need much larger windows (128, 256, 1024 bits or more) to handle packet reordering from multiple crypto cores. The algorithm works at any size and provides the most benefit for large windows.
sections.eli5: This way is faster in two ways: clearing blocks (instead of shifting bits) takes less time, and checking which number is acceptable is a simpler math operation. The downside is needing a small extra buffer, which costs almost nothing for large windows.

sections.title: Compatibility and Deployment
sections.content:
This algorithm is completely transparent to the sender and causes no interoperability issues. The sender sends exactly the same packets with the same sequence numbers. The receiver is free to choose any compliant anti-replay method—whether the standard bit-shifting method or this block-based method—and both will correctly accept packets from each other.

The RFC emphasizes that this algorithm describes receiver-side processing only. The sender does not know or care which algorithm the receiver uses. A receiver can switch from one algorithm to the other without any impact on senders.

However, the RFC warns that deploying this algorithm in networks with significant packet reordering beyond the 32- or 64-bit window is risky. Some existing IPsec implementations do not support large windows or the extended anti-replay processing defined here. Deploying this in such networks could cause packets to be unexpectedly dropped.

The algorithm is an informational RFC, not a standard, so implementations are free to adopt it or stick with the traditional method. Its main value is for manufacturers of high-performance network processors who need efficient anti-replay at scale.
sections.eli5: Senders do not care which method a receiver uses, so adding this does not break anything. But if the network has old IPsec systems that do not understand large windows, they might drop packets by mistake. So it is for advanced systems only, not for everyday use.

left.title: Standard algorithm
left.desc: Shifts all bits in the window when sequence number jumps.

right.title: Block-based algorithm
right.desc: Only clears whole blocks without shifting any bits.
